algorithm: Extract -> transform -> load over synthetic records

classes.desc: Three-stage ETL pipeline for topic records.
classes.name: Pipeline

data_flow_ascii:
generate_raw (extract) -> clean_rows (transform)
clean_rows -> write_csv (load) -> demo_workspace/records_clean.csv
Pipeline.run prints per-stage row counts
description_sentence: Extracts synthetic topic records, transforms them (drop invalid, normalize, bucket), and loads the clean set to CSV.
failure_note: Corrupt rows (null or negative values) are counted and dropped in the transform stage rather than crashing the pipeline; an empty input writes a header-only CSV.

label: Data pipeline (ETL)
output_shape: A stage report table (extracted, dropped, loaded row counts), bucket distribution, five sample rows, and the CSV path.
pitch_sentence: A {topic} ETL pipeline that extracts seeded records, cleans and buckets them, loads a CSV, and reports every stage count.

qa.a: No; generate_raw synthesizes deterministic rows from the seed, so the pipeline demonstrates all three stages with zero external input.
qa.q: Does the pipeline need a real data source?

qa.a: clean_rows drops them, counts the drops, and reports the number in the stage report.
Yes; it is the only file write, and it stays inside the current working directory under demo_workspace/.

resume_bullet_template: Built a {topic} ETL pipeline in Python (stdlib csv) with extract, transform, and load stages; handles corrupt rows with drop counts and reports per-stage statistics to the console.
run_notes: The pipeline writes demo_workspace/records_clean.csv in the current working directory; use --out-dir to change it.
scaling_note: All rows are held in memory between stages, so very large inputs would need chunked or streaming processing instead.
storage_note: The only persistence is the output CSV written to ./demo_workspace; the raw and intermediate rows exist only in memory during the run.
tradeoff_note: In-memory batch processing keeps the code simple and fast for demo sizes, at the cost of not streaming arbitrarily large datasets.
